lesson.title: Decoding: Reading the Signal Back into Bits
lesson.summary: Decoding is the receiver's task of reversing an encoding scheme: sampling a physical signal at the right moments and turning it back into the original bit stream correctly, even when timing and noise are working against it.
lesson.body:
Encoding, as you just saw, is the transmitter's job of turning a bit stream into a physical signal that a medium can actually carry. Decoding is the receiver's matching job on the other end: examine the incoming physical signal, whatever pattern of voltage levels, transitions, or light pulses arrives, and reconstruct the original sequence of bits the transmitter started with. Every encoding scheme has to be paired with a decoding rule that can undo it, and the reliability of an entire communication link often comes down to how well that decoding rule copes with real, imperfect signals rather than clean textbook waveforms.

The core difficulty in decoding is not usually figuring out what a level or transition means once you know where to look, it is knowing exactly where to look. A receiver samples the incoming signal at discrete instants and has to align those sampling instants with the bit boundaries the transmitter used, a problem generally called clock recovery or timing recovery. Some systems solve this with a separate clock signal sent alongside the data, which is simple but wastes a channel. Most systems instead try to recover timing directly from the data signal, which is exactly why self clocking encoding schemes like Manchester encoding matter so much: because every bit period is guaranteed to contain a signal transition, the decoder can use those transitions to continuously correct its notion of where each bit period starts and ends, rather than drifting out of alignment over a long run of unchanging data.

Take a simple worked example using NRZ-L encoding, where a decoder just measures the voltage level once per bit period and reports a 1 for a high level and a 0 for a low level. Suppose the transmitted physical signal, sampled once per bit period, reads high, high, low, high, low, low. A correctly synchronized decoder reports exactly 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0. But suppose the receiver's clock has drifted so its sampling instant falls slightly outside the true bit period, near a transition; it might sample during the wrong bit or catch a transient value between levels, and the decoded bit at that position becomes unreliable. This is precisely why decoders for schemes without guaranteed transitions need extra safeguards, or why designers choose self clocking schemes for links where clock drift is a real risk.

Decoding also has to cope with noise added along the transmission path. A receiver rarely sees the exact voltage the transmitter sent; it sees that voltage plus whatever interference the medium introduced. Decoders handle this with a decision threshold, treating any received value above some midpoint as a 1 and anything below it as a 0, along with filtering that smooths out short noise spikes before the threshold comparison happens. As long as the noise is small relative to the gap between the two signal levels, the decoded bit still comes out correct even though the exact received voltage never quite matches what was sent.

Manchester encoding and NRZ encoding, covered next, are the two concrete schemes you will decode most often in practice, and each demands a slightly different decoding strategy: NRZ decoding is a straightforward level comparison, while Manchester decoding has to identify the direction of the mid bit transition rather than just a static level, which is part of what buys it that built in clocking guarantee.
